content: If an individual’s HIV test results remain unchanged after retesting, they will be diagnosed as HIV-negative. According to the 2019 WHO guidelines on HIV testing services, individuals with an inconclusive HIV status should be retested 14 days later using the same testing strategy and algorithm. If the results resolve to either HIV-positive (e.g., A1+, A2+, A3+) or HIV-negative (e.g., A1−), the diagnosis should be reported accordingly. Retesting should ideally occur at the same site and follow the same testing protocol. Post-test counseling is essential for individuals with inconclusive or negative results, as outlined in Chapter 4 of the guidelines. While most people who test HIV-negative do not require frequent retesting, certain individuals at higher risk may need annual or more frequent testing. Chapters 4 and 7 provide guidance on populations requiring retesting and the associated counseling messages. Periodic retesting is also recommended to detect breakthrough HIV infections (i.e., when HIV is acquired despite PrEP use) as early as possible. Most breakthrough infections occur in individuals who have discontinued PrEP. WHO recommends using the same testing strategy and algorithm for PrEP users as for others. Some clinical trials for PrEP initiation have used assays optimized for detecting acute HIV infection, but these are often more expensive and complex, with limited additional benefit in settings where nucleic acid testing (NAT) or fourth-generation serology assays are not routinely used. In cases of inconclusive HIV results during PrEP use, weekly serology testing for four weeks is recommended. If the serology profile remains unchanged (e.g., A1+, A2+, A3− or A1+, A2−), the individual is considered HIV-negative, and PrEP can be continued with quarterly retesting. If the profile evolves to confirm HIV-positive status (e.g., A1+, A2+, A3+), the diagnosis must be verified before transitioning from PrEP to antiretroviral therapy (ART). This verification should involve a different testing provider, preferably at a different site, using new specimens and test kits. If necessary, PrEP may be discontinued for up to four weeks to allow viral replication and antibody response to develop, with weekly serology and virological testing conducted during this period. Alternative HIV prevention methods, such as condom use, should be strongly recommended during this time. NAT assays are unsuitable for periodic testing of PrEP users because antiretroviral drugs suppress viral replication below detectable levels. The standard testing strategy and algorithm remain the most appropriate for quarterly HIV testing in PrEP users. Community-based testing strategies, such as test for triage and HIV self-testing, are valuable for expanding access to HIV testing, particularly among underserved populations. In the test for triage approach, a trained provider conducts a single rapid diagnostic test (RDT) rather than the full testing algorithm. Reactive results are referred to a facility for confirmatory testing. Similarly, HIV self-testing allows individuals to perform an initial test themselves, with reactive results requiring further confirmatory testing. These strategies reduce stigma and increase access to testing services but are not recommended for individuals with HIV who are already on ART. Integrated testing for other conditions, such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs), syphilis, and hepatitis B, alongside HIV testing, is encouraged. For example, dual HIV/syphilis RDTs can be used in antenatal care settings to improve testing and treatment coverage. Multiplex assays that detect multiple infections, such as HIV, hepatitis C, and hepatitis B, are also being explored. When selecting diagnostic assays, it is critical to prioritize sensitivity for the first test (Assay 1) to identify all HIV-positive individuals, even if this results in some false-reactive results. Subsequent tests (Assay 2 and Assay 3) should prioritize specificity to rule out false-reactive results. In some settings, western blotting and line immunoassays are still used as confirmatory tests, although most HIV diagnoses worldwide rely on RDTs. These laboratory-based technologies are more common in high-income regions and certain parts of Asia and the Middle East, where knowledge of HIV status remains low, hindering ART uptake and prevention efforts. Finally, external factors such as co-infections, immunizations, or therapies can impact HIV test results. For example, individuals co-infected with diseases like dengue or leishmaniasis may exhibit false-reactive HIV results. Similarly, vaccine-induced seroreactivity can lead to false-positive results in individuals participating in vaccine trials. Understanding these limitations is essential for accurate interpretation of HIV test results.
